newsitem.title: USA: Record U.S. refinery runs speeds end to good margins.
newsitem.headline: Record U.S. refinery runs speeds end to good margins.

text.p: Record refinery utilization rates in the United States are likely to hasten the end of the attractive downstream profit margins the oil industry has enjoyed for much of this year, industry participants say.
The extremely high running rate may also raise the dangers of explosions and other disruptions at refineries, as it has in the past, analysts said.

"It's the first time I can ever remember total U.S. capacity being over 100 percent," said Ken Miller, senior principal at Houston-based oil consultancy Purvin & Gertz, referring to data released on Wednesday by the Department of Energy showing refinery utilization rates last week soared to an all-time record of 100.4 percent.

The figure over 100 percent is due to the fact that DOE capacity is on a "calendar day" basis that smooths out over time factors like downtime related to maintenance. On a "stream day" basis, which calculates usage against capacity actually available, utilization was running at about 95 percent.
But analysts said the running rate is still phenomenal.
"You can quibble about the numbers but it appears the U.S. refining industry is running at capacity," said Tom Knight, a refined products trader at Fina Inc., the U.S. unit of Petrofina SA.
Historically, there is a strong correlation between refiners running full out and having production problems.
"If you have a half dozen refinery problems when you're running at 95 percent, then you're likely to have more when you're running at 100 percent," said Purvin & Gertz's Miller.

But the more likely threat to the high running rate is deteriorating economics -- with the high level of production already eating into margins, it's only a matter of time before refiners cut back output to stop the swing back toward loss-making levels.

"From an engineering point of view the high runs are sustainable (but) from a marketing point of view it's another question. I mean, look at the distillate production rates and the gasoline production rates," said Ed Murphy, a statistician with the American Petroleum Institute.
The API on Tuesday reported record gasoline output of nearly 8.2 million bpd and distillate output of 3.7 million bpd, which is high for the season.

U.S. gasoline output has been running at around 7.7 million bpd in the last four weeks, with demand at around 8.1 million bpd, the DOE data show. But imports, drawn in by relatively high U.S. prices, have averaged 658,000 bpd.
"The economic argument is probably going to have more prominence," said Fina's Knight.

Purvin & Gertz's Miller says there may be signs of some underlying improvement in the industry in the fact that it takes such a high level of production before margins are hurt. But he says there is still trouble ahead for the sector.

"It used to be a whole lot easier to overproduce. But the runs are still pretty alarming. We're running more barrels through refineries than ever before in history. And running at these rates, you're asking for extra problems," Miller said.
